Part D · Chapter 1

Tokenisation

How text becomes the whole numbers a language model reads, and why GPT-2's tokenizer needs more tokens for the Hindi and Marathi messages than for the English ones

A language model reads whole numbers, one per token. This chapter builds a tokenizer with byte-pair encoding, one merge at a time, and compares two tokenizers in use. Under GPT-2's tokenizer, the English meaning of one invented report takes 23 tokens and its Hindi text 117.

All sixteen messages are invented. The Hindi, Marathi and Hinglish texts have not yet been checked by a native speaker.

You will need: dictionary lookup (0.2), dictionaries and tuples in Python (0.1) and a feel for Big-O (0.2).

  1. Characters, words or pieces?
  2. Byte-pair encoding, one merge at a time
  3. Using the merges on new text

Characters, words or pieces?

Guess first. A model must read the sentence “Two sharkcams filmed hammerheads at Sassoon Dock.” You can cut it into characters, whole words or pieces of words. Which cut gives the fewest units, which needs the biggest vocabulary (the list of all units the model can use), and which fails on a word it has never seen?

A token is one unit of text that has its own number, and the tokenizer is the program that cuts text into tokens. Cut into characters, the sentence gives the most tokens, but the vocabulary is small and no word is unknown. Cut into words, it gives the fewest tokens, but the vocabulary grows with the data. A word that is missing from it becomes <unk>, a placeholder that hides which word was there. Pieces are parts of words or whole common words. GPT-2’s pieces can write any text, so none of its tokens is unknown.

  1. Switch the first sentence between Characters, Words and GPT-2 pieces: the counts are 49, 8 and 12 tokens, and Words shows 3 <unk> chips.
  2. Press Tag 4128: Words turns 4128 into <unk>, and GPT-2 pieces cut it into ▁4 and 128.
  3. Press Hindi with GPT-2 pieces: 21 characters become 34 tokens, and the coral chips are bytes in hex, only parts of a character.

The first sentence is 49 characters, 8 words with 3 unknown, or 12 GPT-2 pieces with none unknown. The sentences are made up.

How it works

Count the cost of length. Attention is a step of the model, covered later, that compares the tokens of a text with one another. For n tokens it makes about n × n comparisons, so in its usual form its cost grows like n2. The first sentence has n = 49 characters but n = 12 GPT-2 pieces.

n2comparisons:492 = 2,40149 characters÷122 = 14412 pieces=16.7times as many

The ratio is the square of the length ratio, since 49 ÷ 12 is about 4.1 and 4.12 is about 17. Words give the shortest sequence, 8 tokens, but fail differently. The figure’s word list has 79 entries, the words and signs of the four English messages, so it lacks “sharkcams”, “filmed” and “hammerheads”, and all three become <unk>. New words, names, numbers and typos keep appearing, so no word list is complete. A short algorithm learns the pieces from text instead, and the next section runs it.

Common belief. A tokenizer splits text into words.

Why it fails. Tokens can be pieces of different sizes, and GPT-2’s pieces keep common words whole (“▁at”, “▁Dock”) and split rare words into known parts (“▁shark” + “c” + “ams”). The number 4128 becomes “▁4” and “128”, and “sharkcamera” becomes “▁shark” and “camera”. A Devanagari character can be cut into bytes. The mark ▁ means a space before the piece, so “▁shark” and “shark” are different tokens.

Better account. A token is whatever piece the vocabulary contains, so a word may be one token or several and counting words predicts the token count badly.

Quick quiz

A word-level model reads “Tag 4128”. What does it do with 4128?

If 4128 is not in its vocabulary, it replaces the number with <unk>, so the model cannot tell which tag was meant. A piece-level tokenizer writes it as known pieces.

Why not use one token per character?

The vocabulary stays small, but the token sequence is long. Attention makes about n × n comparisons, so its cost grows with the square of the length.

Terms

tokenizer

vocabulary

piece (subword)

Longer sequences, larger vocabularies, spelling variants

Because the cost grows like n2, a sequence five times longer costs about 25 times as much in the attention step (0.2). A character vocabulary for English needs about 100 letters, digits and signs, while Unicode lists over 100,000 characters in all. The word list of the figure is a small version of a full word list. Names, numbers, typos and new spellings keep arriving, so a word vocabulary keeps growing. Hinglish is written in Latin letters, and writers spell it in their own ways, so one word may appear as chhoti and choti, which a word list treats as two different words.

Where this is used

Used in: the sequence length n that attention works on (D4), and the cost of long inputs (D6).

Byte-pair encoding, one merge at a time

Guess first. Words start as rows of single characters, and in one step you may glue two neighbouring symbols into one new symbol, in all the places where the pair occurs. The pair “ha” appears inside shark, sharks, sharkcam, hammerhead and hammerheads. Which pair would you glue first to make the corpus, the training text, shorter, and when would you stop?

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is an algorithm that learns the pieces from the corpus, here a made-up corpus of 15 words with counts. It counts the pairs of neighbouring symbols, weighted by how often their word occurs, and merges the most frequent pair into one new symbol. A merge shortens the corpus by the number of times the pair occurred, so the most frequent pair shortens it most. The algorithm repeats this for a number of merges that a person chooses in advance. Common words become single tokens early, while rare words stay in pieces for longer.

  1. Press Reset, then Step: the coral pair h + a (29 times) becomes ha, and the corpus falls from 408 to 379 pieces.
  2. Press Step four more times: shark becomes the single piece ▁shark (▁ marks the space before the word).
  3. Drag Merges done to 30: the corpus is 99 pieces long, but bamboo is still in five pieces.

The corpus: made-up word counts, with the words cut into pieces

Pair counts: the coral bar is merged next

Five merges turn “shark” into one token; after 30 merges the corpus has 99 pieces instead of 408, but “bamboo” still has five.

How it works

Take the first merge. The pair h + a occurs once in five words: shark, which occurs 10 times in the corpus, sharks (7), sharkcam (5), hammerhead (4) and hammerheads (3). A word counts as often as it occurs, so the pair has a count of 29, the highest of all pairs, and ha joins the vocabulary.

countof the pair h + a:10shark+7sharks+5sharkcam+4hammerhead+3hammerheads=29count of h + a

After a merge the counts change. The row ▁ s h a r k becomes ▁ s ha r k. The pairs s + h, h + a and a + r disappear and the pairs s + ha and ha + r appear, which is why the plot is drawn again after a merge. Merge 2 is ▁ + s with a count of 22 (shark 10, sharks 7, sharkcam 5). Bamboo occurs 3 times, which is low in this corpus, so its pairs have low counts and are merged late.

Analogy. Text-message shorthand: people shorten the phrases they type most, such as “lol”, so common phrases take few symbols.

Where it breaks. People shorten with meaning in mind, while BPE uses counts alone, so a piece such as “▁hammerh” can appear because it was frequent, whatever its meaning. Pieces often look like word parts, as with the plural “s”, because word parts repeat.

Quick quiz

After the merge “h” + “a”, is the pair “s” + “h” still in “shark”?

No. The row is now “▁ s ha r k”, so the pairs are “▁s”, “s ha”, “ha r” and “r k”. A merge removes old pairs and makes new ones.

Does training need the labels or meanings of words?

No. It counts neighbouring pairs in raw text, so it needs no labels.

Go deeper terms, second merge, equation, code, history about 4 min

Terms

pair
two symbols next to one another inside a word
merge
replacing all occurrences of a pair by one new symbol, which joins the vocabulary
byte-pair encoding (BPE)
training a tokenizer by merging the most frequent pair, again and again
merge list
the merges in the order they were learned

How to read the figure

Read the figure in four steps. First, the words are cut into characters, with ▁ marking the space before the word. Second, the plot counts all neighbouring pairs, weighted by how often their word occurs. Third, the most frequent pair is glued together in all words, and the new symbol joins the vocabulary. Fourth, the loop repeats. The dashed outlines in the corpus show where the next merge will happen. When two pairs tie, the one met first in the table wins. Training stops after a chosen number of merges. In this tiny corpus all 15 words are single pieces after 44 merges and no pair is left. A production tokenizer stops much earlier, at a vocabulary size chosen in advance. Press Step to do one merge, Play to watch them run, and Back to undo. The word counts are made up.

A second example

Take a second example by hand. The pair “e” + “r” is merged eighth with a count of 9. It occurs once in hammerhead (4), once in hammerheads (3) and once in diver (2), and \(4 + 3 + 2 = 9\). The equation box of the figure shows the same kind of sum for the pair that is merged next.

The counts as an equation

\[ \mathrm{count}(a,b) \;=\; \sum_{w} f(w)\; c_w(a,b) \qquad\qquad (a^{*}, b^{*}) \;=\; \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{(a,b)} \; \mathrm{count}(a,b) \]

  • \(w\) is a distinct word, \(f(w)\) is how often it occurs in the corpus, and \(c_w(a,b)\) is how many times the symbol \(a\) is directly followed by \(b\) inside \(w\).
  • \((a^{*}, b^{*})\) is the pair with the largest count. It becomes the new symbol \(a^{*}b^{*}\).
  • The vocabulary size is the alphabet size plus the number of merges. Here \(43 + 44 = 87\).

Why counting words works, and what BPE leaves behind

Why does counting words with their frequencies work? Scanning ten copies of “shark” finds the same pair ten times, so counting the word once and multiplying by 10 gives the same total, much faster. Practical implementations do this. The method is greedy: it never looks ahead. The pieces “▁sha” and “▁shar” were useful stepping stones, but after “▁shark” forms they no longer appear in any word. They stay in the vocabulary anyway: of the 44 merged pieces, 15 are whole words and 29 are stepping stones, so the vocabulary of 87 is larger than the list of 15 words. The method began as a way to compress data (Gage, 1994). Sennrich, Haddow and Birch (2016) brought it to machine translation to cope with rare words. The same algorithm trains GPT-2’s tokenizer, with bytes as the alphabet (256 byte symbols, 50,000 merges and one special token make its 50,257 entries).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If two runs on the same text give different vocabularies, check how ties are broken. Production trainers fix a rule (here: first seen). A tie broken at random would give a different tokenizer from one run to the next, and a model works only with the tokenizer it was trained with.

In Python

from collections import Counter

words = {"shark": 10, "sharks": 7, "hammerhead": 4, "dock": 5, "docks": 3}   # made-up counts
corpus = {w: ["▁"] + list(w) for w in words}   # start from characters; ▁ marks the space before a word

def count_pairs(corpus, words):
    pairs = Counter()
    for w, pieces in corpus.items():
        for a, b in zip(pieces, pieces[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += words[w]            # a word counts as often as it occurs
    return pairs

def merge(pieces, pair):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(pieces):
        if i + 1 < len(pieces) and (pieces[i], pieces[i + 1]) == pair:
            out.append(pieces[i] + pieces[i + 1]); i += 2      # glue the pair into one piece
        else:
            out.append(pieces[i]); i += 1
    return out

for step in range(1, 4):
    pairs = count_pairs(corpus, words)
    best, n = pairs.most_common(1)[0]
    corpus = {w: merge(p, best) for w, p in corpus.items()}
    print(f"merge {step}: {best[0]} + {best[1]} -> {best[0] + best[1]}  ({n} times)")
print(corpus["sharks"], corpus["hammerhead"])
merge 1: h + a -> ha  (21 times)
merge 2: ▁ + s -> ▁s  (17 times)
merge 3: ▁s + ha -> ▁sha  (17 times)
['▁sha', 'r', 'k', 's'] ['▁', 'ha', 'm', 'm', 'e', 'r', 'h', 'e', 'a', 'd']

This corpus is smaller than the one in the figure, so its counts differ (21 instead of 29 for “ha”). The first merges still match.

Where this is used

Used in: many language models, GPT-2 among them. The next sections use the merges to cut new text (3) and give the pieces their numbers (4).

Using the merges on new text

Guess first. You trained 44 merges, and someone now types “hammerheads at the dock”. Does the tokenizer need the training corpus, or only the merge list (the merges in the order they were learned)? What will it do with “at”, which never appeared in training?

To encode new text, which means to turn it into tokens, the tokenizer splits the text into words and breaks the words into characters. It then applies the merges in the order they were learned, and it needs the merge list but not the training corpus. Splitting into words first keeps a merge from joining the end of one word to the start of the next. A character that is not in the alphabet (its starting symbols) needs a rule. Byte fallback writes it as its bytes, the numbers a computer stores for it, and the other choice replaces it with <unk>.

  1. Drag Merges used to 0: the text is 24 tokens, 20 letters and 4 ▁ marks.
  2. Press Use all 44: 8 tokens remain, ▁hammerheads and ▁dock whole but “at” and “the” in characters (▁ a t, ▁t h e).
  3. Press the preset छोटी बांस शार्क: Write as bytes gives 42 tokens (3 per character, 3 ▁ marks), and Use <unk> gives 16.

With no merges the text “hammerheads at the dock” takes 24 tokens, and with all 44 merges it takes 8. The small number under a token is its ID.

How it works

Apply the merges to “hammerheads”. The word starts as 12 symbols, ▁ h a m m e r h e a d s. Eleven of the 44 merges apply to it, in the order they were learned. They are merge 1 (h + a), merge 8 (e + r) and merge 18 (▁ + ha). Merges 19 to 25 add m, m, er, h, e, a and d one by one, and merge 29 is ▁hammerhead + s.

lengthof the word:12symbols at the start−11merges that apply=1token, ▁hammerheads

A merge joins two symbols into one, so here the word shrinks by one symbol per merge, from 12 symbols to one token. The word “at” was not in the training corpus, and no merge joins ▁ with a or a with t, so it stays in three tokens, ▁ a t. For “the” only merge 7 (▁ + t) applies, which gives ▁t h e. The order of the merges matters: merge 3 (▁s + ha) joins symbols that merges 1 and 2 made, so applied before them it would have no pair to join.

Common belief. A tokenizer looks up words in a dictionary of words.

Why it fails. The vocabulary contains pieces, and a word the tokenizer has never seen is built from pieces by the merge list; with byte fallback any text can be written.

Better account. The merge list is a recipe for cutting text, and the vocabulary, covered next, gives the pieces their numbers.

Quick quiz

How many tokens does “at” take in the toy tokenizer, and why?

Three: ▁, a and t. The pairs ▁a and at never occur in the training corpus, so no merge joins them.

Does byte fallback lose information?

No. A character outside the alphabet is written as its bytes, and the bytes rebuild the character. It costs more tokens. The option to make letters lower case first does remove capitals.

Terms

encode
turn text into tokens, using the merge list
pre-tokenise
split text into words and signs first, so merges never join two words
byte fallback
writing a character that is not in the alphabet as its UTF-8 bytes
<unk>

What the figure shows

Slide the merges from 0 to 44 and watch the text shrink. Words from the training corpus collapse quickly, and “hammerheads” is one token once its merges are done. “At” and “the” never appeared in training, so they stay as letters, except that the merge ▁ + t turns “the” into “▁t”, “h” and “e”. A tokenizer trained on SharkCam notes would cut ordinary English into many pieces, in the same way that GPT-2’s tokenizer, probably trained on mostly English text, cuts Devanagari (section 7). With the Hindi preset and byte fallback, a Devanagari character becomes three byte tokens and no information is lost. With <unk>, all characters become the same placeholder, and the model cannot tell them apart. The slider and the trainer above share one setting, so the merges stay in step.

Splitting into words first

Most tokenizers in use also split text into words with a pattern before merging, as the figure does. A merge then never joins the end of one word to the start of the next.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A stray space changes the tokens. In GPT-2, “▁shark” is token 21027 but “shark” without a space is two tokens, 1477 and 668. When a prompt behaves oddly, print the tokens, not the text. A model trained with one tokenizer also cannot read the IDs of another, so always load the tokenizer that belongs to the model.

Where this is used

Used in: any call to a language model. Many services charge a prompt by its number of tokens (section 7).

Vocabulary and IDs

Guess first. A model works on numbers, and GPT-2’s vocabulary has 50,257 tokens. Suppose you stored the vocabulary as a list and scanned it from the start, and all tokens were equally likely. About how many comparisons would one lookup need on average, and how many would a dictionary need?

The vocabulary gives a token an ID, a whole number. A dictionary, such as Python’s dict, maps the token to its ID and finds a key in about one step on average, however many keys it has. A list of tokens maps an ID back to its token by position, which is also one step. Encoding looks tokens up in the dictionary, and decoding reads the list, whereas scanning the list to find a token would be much slower.

  1. With 5 or more merges set above, the first box shows ▁shark with ID 307: a list scan would need 308 comparisons, a dictionary 1 step.
  2. Type 307 in the first box: it returns ▁shark, read by position in one step.
  3. At 5 merges, “sharks at the dock” encodes to 14 IDs and decodes to the same text.

The toy vocabulary, with the merges chosen above (click a row)

A list scan needs one comparison per position it passes, so ID 307 costs 308 comparisons, and a dictionary needs one step.

How it works

The toy vocabulary has a fixed layout. IDs 0 to 3 are special tokens, which mark structure. IDs 4 to 259 are the 256 byte values, and IDs 260 to 302 are the 43 symbols of the alphabet. The merged tokens follow in the order of the merges, so the n-th merge has the ID 302 + n. For ▁shark, the fifth merge, that is 302 + 5 = 307, however many merges you use above.

(50,257 + 1) ÷ 2average list scan=25,129comparisons per token×1,000tokens in a text=25,129,000comparisonsvs1,000with a dictionary

Here V = 50,257 is the vocabulary size, so a scan may pass up to V positions. Suppose the token you look for is equally likely to be at any of them. A scan then needs 1 comparison for the first position, 2 for the second and V for the last, which averages (V + 1) ÷ 2. Frequent tokens have small IDs, so a scan over text would stop earlier, but its cost still grows with V.

Common belief. Token IDs have meaning, so nearby IDs are similar words.

Why it fails. An ID is a position in a list that follows the order of the merges. “▁shark” (21027) and “▁sharks” (27476) are far apart in GPT-2.

Better account. An ID is a name, and meaning comes later from the embedding, a list of numbers that the model learns for an ID, which is the next chapter.

Quick quiz

For a text of 1,000 tokens and GPT-2’s vocabulary of 50,257, about how many comparisons do a list scan and a dictionary need?

About 25,129 per token, so 25,129,000 for the text, against about 1,000 for a dictionary.

What ID does the 10th merged token have in the toy vocabulary?

The ID is 302 + 10 = 312, which is the token ▁div.

Terms

ID
the whole number that names a token, its position in the vocabulary
vocabulary
a dictionary from token to ID, plus the list from ID back to token
decode

Layout and lookups

The layout is that of this toy vocabulary. Tokenizers in use differ: in GPT-2 the special token <|endoftext|> has the last ID, 50256. IDs 0 to 3 are special tokens (section 5 explains them). Then come 256 byte tokens for the fallback, then the alphabet, then the merges in the order they were learned. To encode, the tokenizer looks up the tokens in the dictionary. To decode, it uses the IDs as positions in the list and joins the pieces. This is the dictionary lookup of 0.2. Python’s dict finds a key in about one comparison on average however large it is, while a list needs about half its length. The merge sliders choose which merged tokens exist, but not their IDs.

Binary search and the symbols

\[ \text{list scan: } \frac{V+1}{2} \text{ comparisons on average} \qquad \text{dictionary: } \approx 1 \qquad \text{ID} \to \text{token: } 1 \]

  • \(V\) is the vocabulary size. For GPT-2, \(V = 50{,}257\).
  • A sorted list with binary search (0.2) would need at most \(\lfloor\log_2 V\rfloor + 1 = 16\) comparisons. A dictionary still wins, and needs no sorting.

Some GPT-2 IDs

Here are some GPT-2 IDs, found with the tokenizer: “▁shark” is 21027, “▁sharks” is 27476, “▁Dock” is 36444, “▁bamboo” is 37252 and “▁the” is 262. In GPT-2 the IDs of merged tokens follow the order of the merges, so common words got small IDs, because their merges were learned early. The IDs have no meaning by themselves: “▁shark” and “▁sharks” are close in meaning but far apart in ID. The model turns an ID into a list of learned numbers, an embedding, which is the next chapter (D2).

In Python

# a toy vocabulary: token -> ID
vocab = {"<pad>": 0, "<unk>": 1, "<bos>": 2, "<eos>": 3, "▁shark": 4, "s": 5, "▁dock": 6, "▁at": 7}
inverse = {i: t for t, i in vocab.items()}          # ID -> token, to read the model's answer

tokens = ["<bos>", "▁shark", "s", "▁at", "▁dock", "<eos>"]
ids = [vocab.get(t, vocab["<unk>"]) for t in tokens]  # unknown pieces become <unk>
print(ids)
print("".join(inverse[i] for i in ids if i > 3).replace("▁", " "))
print(vocab.get("▁hammerhead", vocab["<unk>"]))
[2, 4, 5, 7, 6, 3]
 sharks at dock

Where this is used

Used in: the embedding table has one row per ID (D2), and the model's output has one score per ID (D3).

More questions

Why does decoding (ID to token) need no dictionary?

An ID is already a position in a list, so reading the token is one index step, with no hashing.

What is the unknown token ID for, if byte fallback exists?

Tokenizers without byte fallback need it for any character outside the alphabet. Byte-level tokenizers such as GPT-2’s do not need it for text.

Special tokens

Guess first. Four reports are processed together, as one rectangle of numbers, and under GPT-2’s tokenizer they have 27, 179, 193 and 44 tokens. What must be added so that the rows have the same length, and how can the model tell the filler from the text?

A model reads a batch, several texts processed together, as a rectangle of numbers, so all rows need the same length. The short rows are filled up with padding, the special token <pad>. A mask, a list that marks the padding slots, tells attention (the step in which tokens are compared, covered later in this part) to skip them. Special tokens are vocabulary entries that mark structure and are not part of the text. They include padding, start and end tokens that mark where a text begins and ends, and chat tokens that mark who is speaking.

  1. The four rows are the reports m03, m07, m11 and m15; coral marks start and end, teal the text, outlined slots the padding: 329 of 780 slots, or 42%.
  2. Press Qwen2.5: the longest row falls from 195 to 120 slots, and the padding to 35%.
  3. Press No padding: the rows keep their own lengths and no longer form a rectangle.

Padding the four young-hammerhead reports to the longest one makes 42% of the slots padding under GPT-2, because the Marathi report has 193 tokens and the English one 27.

How it works

Count the padding. With the start and end tokens added, the four rows have 29, 181, 195 and 46 slots. The longest row, the Marathi one, has 195, so the batch has 4 × 195 = 780 slots. The rows use 29 + 181 + 195 + 46 = 451 of them, and the other 780 − 451 = 329 slots are padding.

slotsin the batch:4 × 195 = 780slots in the batch−451slots used by reports=329padding slots: 329 ÷ 780 = 42%

The model still processes the padding slots, so the compute spent on them is wasted, and training code often groups reports of similar length into one batch. Other special tokens mark the edges of a text. GPT-2 has <|endoftext|>, which marks the start and the end of a document, and Qwen2.5 adds <|im_start|> and <|im_end|>, which mark the beginning and end of a turn in a chat. A model learns to produce the end token when a reply is finished, and generation stops there.

Common belief. Padding is harmless, because it is filler that adds no information to the text.

Why it fails. A pad slot has a token with an ID. If attention is not told to skip it, the model reads it as part of the text, and a short report can get different results when it is batched with long ones.

Better account. Padding is safe when a mask hides it, but it also costs compute, so batch similar lengths together.

Quick quiz

Four rows have 10, 20, 30 and 40 tokens. How many slots are padding if the batch is padded to 40?

Slots total 4 × 40 = 160. Message tokens total 100. Padding is 60 slots, or 37.5%.

What does the mask do, and what does it not save?

The mask tells attention to skip the padding slots, so the padding does not change the result. The padding slots are still processed, so the compute spent on them is not saved.

Terms

special token
a vocabulary entry that marks structure instead of standing for text
padding (<pad>)
filler that makes short rows as long as the longest one
start and end (<bos>, <eos>)
tokens that mark where a text begins and ends
chat tokens
tokens that mark who is speaking in a conversation

Another tokenizer, less padding

Switch the tokenizer to Qwen2.5 and the padding share falls to 35%, because its tokens for Hindi and Marathi are fewer. For all four topics of the figure the share is lower under Qwen2.5 than under GPT-2. A model reads a batch as a rectangle, so all rows must have the same length. The short rows get <pad> tokens. A mask tells attention to skip them (D4).

The special tokens of the two tokenizers

Other special tokens give the text edges. GPT-2 has just one, <|endoftext|> with ID 50256. It marks both the start and the end of a document. Qwen2.5’s tokenizer has this token (151643). It also has <|im_start|> (151644) and <|im_end|> (151645), which mark the beginning and end of a turn in a chat, together with a role such as “user”. A model learns to emit the end token when a reply is finished, and generation stops there (D3).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model never stops talking, check that the end token is added to the training text and that generation stops on it. If results change when you batch, check the padding mask first.

Where this is used

Used in: attention masks (D4), the generation loop (D3) and chat assistants (D7).

Bytes, characters and scripts

Guess first. The letter “s” takes one byte in a computer file. How many bytes does the Devanagari character “श” (sha) take?

A byte is a number from 0 to 255. UTF-8, the usual way to store text, writes a code point (the number that Unicode gives a character) as one to four bytes. An English letter takes one byte and a Devanagari character takes three. A byte-level tokenizer uses the 256 byte values as its alphabet, so it can write any text. For Hindi and Marathi the starting row is longer, 2.5 to 2.6 bytes per character in these messages, and merges have to shorten it.

  1. The table lists the 11 characters of शार्क shark: a Devanagari character takes 3 UTF-8 bytes (E0 A4 B6 for श), the space and letters 1, so 21 bytes, 1.91 per character.
  2. Press Hindi m05 and then Marathi m09: 77 characters need 193 bytes (2.51 per character) and 74 characters need 194 bytes (2.62).
  3. Press English m01: 170 characters and 170 bytes, 1.00 per character.

English m01 has 170 characters and 170 bytes, Hindi m05 has 77 characters and 193 bytes, and Marathi m09 has 74 characters and 194 bytes.

How it works

Count the bytes of the Hindi message m05. It has 77 characters: 58 Devanagari characters, which take 3 bytes, and 19 others (15 spaces and 4 digits), which take 1 byte. That gives 58 × 3 + 19 × 1 = 193 bytes, or 193 ÷ 77 = 2.51 bytes per character, below 3 because the spaces and digits take one byte.

bytesof message m05:58 × 3 = 174bytes of Devanagari characters+19 × 1 = 19bytes of spaces and digits=193bytes in m05

The code point of s is U+0073, below 128, so one byte is enough. The Devanagari code points run from U+0900 to U+097F, and UTF-8 stores code points from U+0800 to U+FFFF in three bytes. For example, श is U+0936 and its bytes are 224, 164 and 182, written E0 A4 B6 in hex (base 16). A byte-level tokenizer such as GPT-2’s starts from these bytes, so it can write any string with no unknown token. A token can then be a part of a character, such as the hex piece E0 A4 in the first figure.

Common belief. A character is one byte, so the length of a text in characters is also its length in bytes.

Why it fails. That is true for English letters, but message m05 has 77 characters and 193 bytes.

Better account. A character takes one to four bytes in UTF-8, and a byte-level tokenizer starts from the bytes, so count bytes, not characters.

Quick quiz

Message m09 has 60 Devanagari characters, 12 spaces and 2 full stops. How many UTF-8 bytes does it have?

It has 60 × 3 + 14 × 1 = 194 bytes. The Devanagari characters take 3 bytes and the spaces and full stops 1 byte.

If a byte-level tokenizer had no merges for Devanagari, how many tokens would m09 need?

It would need 194, one per byte. GPT-2 used 118, so its merges joined some bytes, to about 1.6 bytes per token.

Go deeper terms, GPT-2 and bytes, Python, debug tip about 2 min

Terms

Unicode
a table that gives all characters a number, its code point
UTF-8
the usual way to store code points as one to four bytes
byte
a number from 0 to 255
byte-level BPE
BPE whose alphabet is the 256 byte values, so any text can be tokenised

Reading the figure

Press the preset buttons to see the difference. Spaces, ASCII digits and full stops take one byte, which lowers the average from 3 to 2.51 bytes per character for the Hindi messages and 2.60 for the Marathi messages (the sign । is Devanagari and takes three bytes). GPT-2 learned many merges for English and few for Devanagari, probably because its training text was mostly English. Radford and colleagues chose bytes so that the model can write any string, with no unknown token. That choice is why the Hindi preset in section 1 was cut into hex pieces such as E0 A4. These are the first two bytes of a character, and they are not a character. Tokenizers also differ in numbers: GPT-2 writes “▁80” as one token, while Qwen2.5 cuts numbers into single digits and writes it as ▁, 8 and 0.

In Python

for text in ["shark", "शार्क"]:
    b = text.encode("utf-8")
    print(f"{text}: {len(text)} characters, {len(b)} bytes")
    print("   bytes in hex:", b.hex(" "))
shark: 5 characters, 5 bytes
   bytes in hex: 73 68 61 72 6b
शार्क: 5 characters, 15 bytes
   bytes in hex: e0 a4 b6 e0 a4 be e0 a4 b0 e0 a5 8d e0 a4 95

Common mistakes

Debug tip. len(text) counts characters, and len(text.encode("utf-8")) counts bytes. A byte-level tokenizer cares about the second number, so do not estimate tokens from character counts, least of all for Hindi, Marathi or emoji.

Where this is used

Used in: the cost comparison across languages in the next section.

Why some languages cost more

Guess first. Under GPT-2’s tokenizer, the English meaning (a translation) of an invented researcher’s report (Tag 4127 at Juhu) takes 45 tokens. The report’s Hindi text is cut into tokens too, and so is its Hinglish text (Hindi written in Latin letters). Guess the token count of the Hindi text (50, 100 or 200), and say whether the Hinglish text takes more or fewer tokens than 45.

The number of tokens depends on the language, the script and the tokenizer. The cost ratio of a message is its number of tokens divided by the number of tokens of its English meaning. Under GPT-2’s tokenizer the mean cost ratio is 5.5 for the four Hindi messages, 4.9 for the four Marathi messages and 1.35 for the four Hinglish messages. All sixteen messages are invented, and the Hindi, Marathi and Hinglish texts have not yet been checked by a native speaker.

  1. Compare the bars: the Hindi and Marathi rows are longest, and coral pieces are parts of characters shown in hex.
  2. The working under the rows is for the Hindi row: 227 ÷ 45 = 5.0 and 227 ÷ 32 = 7.1.
  3. Press Qwen2.5: Hindi falls to 146 tokens and Marathi to 154.

GPT-2 cuts the Tag 4127 messages into 40 tokens in English, 227 in Hindi, 236 in Marathi and 50 in Hinglish; Qwen2.5 gives 146 for Hindi and 154 for Marathi.

How it works

Take the Hindi message m06. Under GPT-2 it takes 227 tokens, and its English meaning takes 45 (the figure’s English row, 40 tokens, is a separate message). The cost ratio ρ (rho) is the first number divided by the second, so ρ = 227 ÷ 45 = 5.0. The message has 32 words, so its fertility, the tokens per word, is 227 ÷ 32 = 7.1. GPT-2’s context window, the most tokens it reads at once, is 1,024, which fits 4 messages like m06 but 22 like its English meaning.

GPT-2Hindi m06:227tokens, Hindi m06÷45tokens, its English meaning=5.0cost ratio ρ|227tokens÷32words=7.1tokens per word

There are four likely causes. First, GPT-2’s merges were probably learned from mostly English text, so English words became single tokens. Second, a Devanagari character is three bytes (bytes section), so a character without merges starts as three tokens. Third, many Hinglish words are not English words: lagbhag and chhoti are both cut into three pieces. Fourth, Marathi joins endings onto words: message m11 begins with वर्सोव्याजवळ (“near Versova”), one word that GPT-2 cuts into 23 pieces.

Common belief. A token is about four characters, or three quarters of a word.

Why it fails. That rule fits English: in the four English messages GPT-2 averages 4.1 characters per token. For the Hindi and Marathi messages it is between 0.6 and 0.7, and for Hinglish 2.8.

Better account. Count tokens with the tokenizer of the model you will call.

Quick quiz

The Hinglish message m14 takes 50 tokens, and its English meaning takes 45. What is ρ?

ρ = 50 ÷ 45 = 1.1. Hinglish costs about 11% more tokens than its English meaning for this message, far less than Hindi in its own script (5.0 for m06).

Give two likely reasons Marathi messages take more tokens than English ones.

The merges were probably learned from mostly English text, so there are few Devanagari merges, and a Devanagari character starts as three bytes. Long Marathi words with attached endings are also cut into many pieces.

Go deeper terms, tokenizers, formulas, studies, debug tip about 3 min

Terms

fertility
tokens per word, a measure of how finely a language is cut
cost ratio \(\rho\)
tokens of a text divided by tokens of its English meaning
context window
the most tokens a model can read at once (GPT-2: 1,024; D3)

Check before reuse

Check before reuse. The Hindi, Marathi and Hinglish texts were written for this primer and have not yet been checked by a native speaker. The English meaning of a message is given in the data file (tokens.json) and is the baseline for the cost ratio. The counts illustrate how two tokenizers cut these texts. They do not measure how fishers write.

The two tokenizers

Compare the four rows for one topic, then press the other tokenizer button. The two tokenizers are open ones: GPT-2 (OpenAI, MIT licence) and Qwen2.5 (Alibaba Cloud, Apache-2.0 licence for the 0.5B model used here). Both use byte-level BPE. The counts were computed offline with the two tokenizers. Qwen2.5 has 151,643 ordinary tokens (Qwen Team, 2024). Writers also spell Hinglish in their own ways (chhoti, choti), and whether that raises the token count is an open question that the exercises return to. The Marathi word of m11 is long because Marathi joins endings onto words, and GPT-2’s merges probably have few pieces for long words like it.

Another worked case

A second worked case is m09: 118 tokens against 27 gives \(\rho = 4.4\), and Qwen2.5 brings the same message to \(72 / 31 = 2.3\). The working below the rows in the figure follows your click on a row.

The formulas

\[ \rho \;=\; \frac{n_{\text{text}}}{n_{\text{English meaning}}} \qquad\qquad \text{fertility} \;=\; \frac{n_{\text{tokens}}}{n_{\text{words}}} \]

  • \(n_{\text{text}}\) is the number of tokens of the message in its own language and \(n_{\text{English meaning}}\) is the number for its English meaning.
  • \(\rho = 1\) means the language is as cheap as English. The values in the chart are for this tokenizer and these twelve short messages only.

Why it matters

Why does it matter? A model reads at most a fixed number of tokens at once, so a Hindi report uses up the window about five times faster. Many commercial services charge by the token. Ahia and colleagues (2023) tested 22 languages and showed that the same content costs very different amounts in OpenAI’s API. Petrov and colleagues (2023) found gaps of up to about 15 times between languages, even with tokenizers meant for many languages. A possible fix is a tokenizer trained on more balanced text. The mean cost ratio of the four Hindi messages is about 3.1 under Qwen2.5 against 5.5 under GPT-2, but Qwen2.5 also has three times the vocabulary, so these counts do not show which difference matters. Qwen2.5 cuts numbers into single digits, which accounts for the extra tokens of its four English messages (42, 45, 29 and 31 against 37, 40, 27 and 27): all of them in m02, m03 and m04, and four of the five in m01. In m03, for example, the number 80 takes 3 tokens against 1. A larger vocabulary has a cost, because the embedding table gets a row per token (D2). For SharkCam this matters because the messages arrive in four languages, and the number of tokens affects the cost in memory, time and money.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a prompt in Hindi or Marathi is cut off or costs more than you planned, count its tokens with the model's own tokenizer before anything else. An estimate from words can be off by a factor of five.

Where this is used

Used in: the context window (D3) and the loss per token (D3), where the same Hindi and Marathi reports look surprisingly easy. This chapter explains why.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory Do three BPE merges by hand. The corpus is ▁tag × 4, ▁tags × 3, ▁tagged × 2 and ▁tide × 3 (made-up counts), with the words cut into characters and a leading ▁. For a merge, write the pair counts, the pair chosen and the new rows. Break ties by the pair first met when reading the words in this order.

    Hint

    Start with the pair ▁ + t. Which words contain it? Then count t + a and a + g.

  2. theory GPT-2's vocabulary has \(V = 50{,}257\) entries. (a) A list scan needs about \((V+1)/2\) comparisons per lookup. How many comparisons does a 800-token text need? (b) How many does binary search over a sorted list need per token? (c) Give one reason why tokenizers still use dictionaries.

  3. theory The Hindi report m05 has 77 characters, 193 bytes and 16 words. GPT-2 cuts it into 117 tokens, and its English meaning into 23. Compute the cost ratio, the bytes per token, the fertility, and the number of reports of both kinds that fit in a 1,024-token window. If attention cost grows like \(n^2\), how many times more does the Hindi report cost in that step?

  4. theory Explain why a BPE vocabulary can contain pieces, such as ▁sha, that never appear in a finished segmentation. Is that a waste? Suggest one way to avoid it.

Practice

  1. practice Write train_bpe(words, n_merges) in Python for the 15 words of the trainer, with the counts shown in the figure (shark 10, sharks 7 and so on). Print the first eight merges and check them against the trainer.

  2. practice Write encode(text, merges) that applies the merges in order, with byte fallback for characters outside the alphabet. Test it on “sharks”, “hammerheads” and a word not in the corpus. Then encode the Hindi word शार्क and check that decoding returns it.

  3. practice Load tokens.json with the json module. Per language and per tokenizer, compute the mean cost ratio and the mean tokens per word, and check them against the chart. Which message has the highest ratio under Qwen2.5?

Think deeper

  1. open A fisher in Uran writes Hinglish with a spelling of their own, and another fisher spells the same words differently: chhoti, choti, chotti. SharkCam must read such messages. How would you measure whether spelling variety hurts the tokenizer? What could you do about it, and what could go wrong with these fixes?

    Hint

    Think of counting tokens per word on the same sentence spelled several ways, and of what normalising spelling would do to a rare local word.

  2. open A service charges per token. A Marathi-speaking fisher and an English-speaking researcher send the same report. Who pays more with GPT-2's tokenizer? Design a fairer pricing rule and say who gains and who loses under it.

  3. open You will train a tokenizer only on SharkCam messages. Choose a vocabulary of 500, 5,000 or 50,000 pieces. What do you gain and lose at these sizes, in sequence length, in the size of the embedding table and in rare words? What experiment would you run to decide?

Come back later

Try these after two days, and again after a week, without looking back.

Why is a tokenizer's vocabulary a dictionary and not a plain list? (Chapter 0.2)

A dictionary finds a key in about one step however large it is. A list scan needs about half its length, which is 25,000 comparisons for 50,257 tokens.

A Hindi report needs 5 times as many tokens as the English one. By how much does attention cost grow for that report? (Chapter 0.2)

Attention cost grows with the square of the length, so about 25 times.

A model with a 50,257-token vocabulary starts training by giving all tokens the same probability. What loss does it start with, and why? (Chapter 0.7)

The loss is \(-\ln(1/50{,}257) = \ln 50{,}257 \approx 10.82\). Equal probabilities give the true token a probability of \(1/V\).
